texts.0: SP, due to incomplete memorization of the critical action procedures, did not state the BOLD FACE steps by heart in the printed sequence and without mistakes. Three memory items of the requested procedure were omitted and two were given out of order, and the recitation stopped before the last step on both attempts. IP had to state the remaining steps from the Check List for the procedure to be completed. Knowledge of the critical action procedures was below the level required to fly the sortie.
texts.1: SP, due to weak recall of the printed wording, did not state the BOLD FACE steps by heart without mistakes. Two steps were reversed and one was paraphrased instead of quoted verbatim, and SP restored the correct sequence only after repeated verbal prompts, about ten seconds after the first error. The procedure was finally stated in full, but at the lower limit of the standard and only with prompting from IP.
texts.2: SP, due to hesitation at the transition between memory items, did not deliver the BOLD FACE sequence at the required pace. One step was initially stated out of order and the recitation paused for about five seconds. SP recognized the break without any prompt, restarted from the preceding step and completed the procedure in the printed order and wording, with no intervention by IP.
texts.3: SP stated the critical action procedures by heart, in the printed sequence, without omissions, additions or paraphrase. Recall was immediate on every procedure requested and the wording matched the Check List exactly. SP kept the same accuracy for the procedures requested in flight as for those requested on the ground.
texts.4: SP recited every BOLD FACE procedure requested, on the ground and in flight, word for word and with no hesitation between items. SP also identified without prompting the point at which the memory items end and the amplified Check List procedure begins. Recall accuracy was equally precise on the rarely practiced procedures.
texts.marginal: SP stated all BOLD FACE steps in the printed sequence and within standards, but recall on the less frequently practiced procedures was noticeably slower and required a short pause before each item. The tendency is toward reconstructing the steps rather than reciting them from memory, which will not hold under the workload of an actual emergency. SP is expected to bring all critical action procedures to immediate recall pace in the coming sorties.

texts_at.1: SP stated the BOLD FACE steps by heart in the printed sequence inside the code 1 band, the correct sequence restored only after repeated prompting on one procedure. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to bring all critical action procedures to immediate recall pace so no prompting is needed.
texts_at.2: SP stated the BOLD FACE steps by heart in the printed sequence inside the code 2 band, correcting one step initially stated out of order after a brief pause. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to shorten that pause so the recall is immediate rather than reconstructed.
texts_at.3: SP stated the critical action procedures by heart, in the printed sequence, without omissions, additions or paraphrase, with recall on one less frequently practiced procedure a little slower than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring that procedure to the same pace as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a break in the recitation without any prompt, restarted from the preceding step and completed the procedure in the printed order and wording, with no intervention by IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good bold face recall.
texts_above.3: SP stated the critical action procedures by heart, in the printed sequence, without omissions, additions or paraphrase, with recall immediate on every procedure requested and the wording matching the Check List exactly. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good bold face recall.
texts_above.4: SP recited every BOLD FACE procedure requested, on the ground and in flight, word for word and with no hesitation between items, identifying without prompting where the memory items end and the amplified checklist begins. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent bold face recall.

error_modes.label: CHECK LIST / IFG EXECUTION AND STANDARDIZED SEQUENCE

texts.0: SP, due to insufficient familiarity with the layout of the Check List, did not execute the amplified procedure according to Check List and IFG in the standardized sequence. Two items were actioned out of order and one complete step was skipped, and the procedure was left unfinished at the point where the landing configuration had to be selected. IP intervened, took over the Check List and directed the remaining steps to completion. Execution was neither flawless nor timely.
texts.1: SP, due to a checklist not followed correctly after the memory items were completed, did not execute the amplified procedure in the standardized sequence. Two steps were performed in reverse order and the transition to the IFG page came about fifteen seconds late, so that the procedure was still open when the aircraft reached the point at which it had to be complete. SP restored the correct sequence only after IP called out each remaining item in turn.
texts.2: SP, due to a rushed transition from the memory items to the amplified procedure, initially read the wrong Check List page for the malfunction being worked. SP detected the discrepancy within about five seconds, returned to the correct procedure and completed all steps in the standardized sequence without IP intervention. Total execution time remained inside the window required for the procedure.
texts.3: SP executed the procedure according to Check List and IFG, without IP intervention, flawlessly, timely and in the standardized sequence. Every step was actioned and confirmed in the printed order, and the transition from memory items to the amplified procedure was made without delay.
texts.4: SP executed all procedures according to Check List and IFG with no intervention, no omissions and no reordering, and completed each one well inside the required time. SP confirmed each switch position against the printed step before moving on, and kept the same standard on the second, unbriefed malfunction of the sortie.
texts.marginal: SP executed the amplified procedures in the standardized sequence and within standards, but relied on reading each step twice before actioning it, which left the procedure only just complete by the required point. The tendency is toward pace that depends on low workload rather than on procedural familiarity. SP is expected to consolidate the Check List and IFG flow so that timing does not degrade when the emergency is combined with pattern work.

texts_at.1: SP executed the amplified procedure according to Check List and IFG in the standardized sequence inside the code 1 band, the correct sequence restored only after each remaining item was called out. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to consolidate the Check List and IFG flow so timing does not degrade under combined workload.
texts_at.2: SP executed the amplified procedure according to Check List and IFG in the standardized sequence inside the code 2 band, correcting a page initially read for the wrong malfunction within a few seconds. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to confirm the correct page before beginning the transition from the memory items.
texts_at.3: SP executed the procedure according to Check List and IFG, without IP intervention, timely and in the standardized sequence, with the transition from memory items to the amplified procedure made a little more deliberately on one occasion than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to make that transition as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP detected a discrepancy in the checklist page within seconds, returned to the correct procedure and completed all steps in the standardized sequence without IP intervention, inside the required time window. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound checklist and IFG execution.
texts_above.3: SP executed the procedure according to Check List and IFG, without IP intervention, flawlessly, timely and in the standardized sequence, actioning and confirming every step in the printed order with the transition from memory items made without delay. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed checklist and IFG execution.
texts_above.4: SP executed all procedures according to Check List and IFG with no intervention, no omissions and no reordering, completing each one well inside the required time and confirming each switch position against the printed step before moving on. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional checklist and IFG execution.

error_modes.label: OBSERVANCE OF AIRCRAFT LIMITS DURING THE EMERGENCY

texts.0: SP, due to attention directed entirely at the Check List steps, did not know and observe the aircraft limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual while working the procedure. SP lowered the landing gear about twenty-five knots above the published maximum gear extension speed and then selected landing flaps above the flap limit speed. IP intervened, retracted the gear and took control to bring the aircraft back inside the published limits.
texts.1: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the limits applicable to the configuration change, did not observe the maximum landing gear extension speed reported in Section V of the Flight Manual and selected the gear about ten knots fast. SP reduced airspeed back inside the limit only after IP called the exceedance, roughly eight seconds later. The remaining configuration changes were made inside the limits, but each one required a verbal reminder of the applicable speed.
texts.2: SP, due to a delayed power reduction while completing the memory items, allowed airspeed to build toward the maximum flap extension speed before the configuration change. SP recognized the trend before the limit was reached, delayed flap selection and reduced airspeed by about ten knots, so that every configuration change stayed inside the published values with no IP input.
texts.3: SP knew and observed the aircraft limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual throughout the procedure. All configuration changes were made inside the published gear and flap speeds, and engine and airframe parameters were kept within limits while the malfunction was being worked.
texts.4: SP observed every applicable Section V limit throughout the emergency and stated the relevant limiting value before each configuration change. Airspeed at gear and flap selection was set with a comfortable margin below the published maximum, and no parameter approached a limit at any point in the procedure.
texts.marginal: SP kept all parameters inside the Section V limits, but configuration changes were made close to the published maximum speeds and the margin depended on IP not extending the profile further. The tendency is toward managing the limit reactively rather than planning the energy so the limit is never approached. SP is expected to establish the target airspeed for each configuration change before selecting it in the coming sorties.

texts_at.1: SP observed the aircraft limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual inside the code 1 band, airspeed brought back inside the limit only after the exceedance was called. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to establish the target airspeed for each configuration change before selecting it.
texts_at.2: SP observed the aircraft limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual inside the code 2 band, correcting an airspeed trend recognized before the flap limit was reached. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize the trend a little earlier so the margin to the limit stays wider.
texts_at.3: SP knew and observed the aircraft limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual throughout the procedure, with all configuration changes made inside the published gear and flap speeds except one made close to the maximum. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to build the same margin into that change as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized an airspeed trend approaching the flap extension limit before it was reached, delayed the selection and reduced airspeed so every configuration change stayed inside published values with no IP input. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady observance of aircraft limits during the emergency.
texts_above.3: SP knew and observed the aircraft limits reported in Section V of the Flight Manual throughout the procedure, keeping all configuration changes inside the published gear and flap speeds with engine and airframe parameters held within limits throughout. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate observance of aircraft limits during the emergency.
texts_above.4: SP observed every applicable Section V limit throughout the emergency, stating the relevant limiting value before each configuration change and setting airspeed with a comfortable margin below the published maximum at all times. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary observance of aircraft limits during the emergency.

error_modes.label: SYSTEMS KNOWLEDGE AND DAILY ASSIGNMENT PREPARATION

texts.0: SP, due to lack of knowledge of the published procedure for the condition encountered, did not know in detail the emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as the daily assignment. SP could not describe the indications associated with the malfunction and answered four of six briefing questions on the affected system incorrectly. IP had to teach the system on the ground before the sortie could continue, and the assignment was repeated.
texts.1: SP, due to insufficient knowledge of the system reversion logic, did not describe in detail the consequences of the malfunction on the associated systems. SP identified the cockpit indications correctly but could explain the follow-on effects only after IP guided the answer step by step. The daily assignment was covered at the lower limit of the standard and required prompting on every second question.
texts.2: SP, due to preparation that concentrated on the memory items rather than on the system, first gave an incomplete account of why the procedure requires the affected switch to be cycled. SP recognized the gap, referred to the correct paragraph and completed the explanation without further input from IP. All remaining questions on the daily assignment were answered accurately at the first attempt.
texts.3: SP knew in detail all emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as the daily assignment. SP described the cockpit indications, the affected components and the reason for each step of the procedure, and answered every briefing question correctly.
texts.4: SP answered every question on the emergency procedures and the associated systems accurately and without hesitation, including the secondary effects on other systems. SP related each step of the procedure to the system behavior it addresses and identified the conditions under which the procedure does not apply. Preparation clearly went beyond the material set as the daily assignment.
texts.marginal: SP knew the emergency procedures and the relevant systems to the required standard, but answers on system interactions were general where specific component behavior was expected. The tendency is toward memorizing the procedure without the system knowledge that supports decisions when the indications are ambiguous. SP is expected to study the affected systems in the depth set by the daily assignment before the next sortie.

texts_at.1: SP knew the emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as the daily assignment inside the code 1 band, the follow-on effects of one malfunction explained only after guidance was given step by step. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to study the affected systems in the depth the daily assignment sets before the next sortie.
texts_at.2: SP knew the emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as the daily assignment inside the code 2 band, correcting an incomplete account of one switch requirement after recognizing the gap unaided. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to prepare that item to the same depth as the rest of the assignment.
texts_at.3: SP knew in detail all emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as the daily assignment, describing the cockpit indications, affected components and reasons for each step, with one explanation drawn a little more slowly than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to bring that explanation to the same readiness as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a gap in an initial explanation, referred to the correct paragraph and completed the explanation without further input from IP, answering the remaining questions accurately at the first attempt. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable systems knowledge for the daily assignment.
texts_above.3: SP knew in detail all emergency procedures and the relevant systems set as the daily assignment, describing the cockpit indications, the affected components and the reason for each step of the procedure and answering every briefing question correctly. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good systems knowledge for the daily assignment.
texts_above.4: SP answered every question on the emergency procedures and the associated systems accurately and without hesitation, including the secondary effects on other systems, and identified the conditions under which the procedure does not apply. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior systems knowledge for the daily assignment.

error_modes.label: AIRCRAFT CONTROL PRIORITY WHILE WORKING THE PROBLEM

texts.0: SP, due to an attention bottleneck on a single caution indication at the expense of the instrument cross-check, did not handle the emergency procedure effectively and stopped flying the aircraft while working the steps. Altitude decayed by about 700 feet, airspeed dropped some 25 knots below the briefed value and heading wandered more than 30 degrees with the wings left in a shallow bank. IP took control to recover the aircraft state before the procedure could be resumed.
texts.1: SP, due to absorption in the cockpit indication that left the descent rate unmonitored, did not maintain the aircraft state while executing the procedure. Altitude decreased by about 300 feet and airspeed fell some 15 knots below the briefed value, reaching the limit of the acceptable deviation. SP returned to the briefed altitude and airspeed only after IP called both deviations, about ten seconds after they developed.
texts.2: SP, due to a short interruption of the instrument cross-check at the start of the procedure, allowed the aircraft to drift about 150 feet low and 10 knots slow. SP detected the deviation on the next scan cycle, corrected altitude and airspeed while continuing the procedure and re-established the cross-check without any input from IP. The procedure was completed with the aircraft back on the briefed parameters.
texts.3: SP handled the emergency procedure effectively while continuing to fly the aircraft. Altitude, airspeed and heading were held on the briefed values throughout the procedure, and the instrument cross-check was maintained between Check List steps.
texts.4: SP flew the aircraft precisely throughout the emergency, with no perceptible change in altitude, airspeed or heading while the procedure was being worked. SP interleaved each Check List step with a full cross-check and kept the aircraft positioned for a suitable forced landing field at all times.
texts.marginal: SP kept the aircraft within the required parameters while working the procedure, but the cross-check narrowed each time a switch had to be selected and the parameters were recovered only at the end of each step. The tendency is toward sequential rather than parallel task handling, which will not hold if the workload increases. SP is expected to keep a continuous scan running between Check List items in the coming sorties.

texts_at.1: SP handled the emergency procedure while continuing to fly the aircraft inside the code 1 band, altitude and airspeed returned to the briefed values only after both deviations were called. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep a continuous scan running between Check List items in the coming sorties.
texts_at.2: SP handled the emergency procedure while continuing to fly the aircraft inside the code 2 band, correcting a brief drift detected on the next scan cycle while the procedure continued. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to shorten the interruption of the cross-check at the start of the procedure.
texts_at.3: SP handled the emergency procedure effectively while continuing to fly the aircraft, holding altitude, airspeed and heading on the briefed values with the cross-check maintained between Check List steps except one step where it narrowed briefly. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to hold that scan open at that step as well.

texts_above.2: SP detected a brief drift on the next scan cycle, corrected altitude and airspeed while continuing the procedure and re-established the cross-check without any input from IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured aircraft control priority while working the problem.
texts_above.3: SP handled the emergency procedure effectively while continuing to fly the aircraft, holding altitude, airspeed and heading on the briefed values throughout the procedure and maintaining the instrument cross-check between Check List steps. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise aircraft control priority while working the problem.
texts_above.4: SP flew the aircraft precisely throughout the emergency, with no perceptible change in altitude, airspeed or heading while the procedure was being worked and each Check List step interleaved with a full cross-check. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate aircraft control priority while working the problem.

error_modes.label: CREW COORDINATION AND DECLARATION OF THE EMERGENCY

texts.0: SP, due to absent explicit role assignment when the malfunction occurred, did not handle the emergency effectively as a crew and left it unclear who was flying and who was working the procedure. No transfer of aircraft control was stated, no emergency was declared to ATC and the intentions were never passed to the front cockpit. IP had to state positive control of the aircraft, declare the emergency and direct the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to an unstated transfer of aircraft control between cockpits, did not coordinate the execution of the procedure with IP. The declaration of the emergency was made about thirty seconds late and the intentions were passed only in fragments, so IP had to ask twice what SP intended to do. Control and task allocation were finally clear, but only after IP prompted each element.
texts.2: SP, due to delayed role allocation in the first seconds after the abnormal indication, initially worked the Check List without stating who was flying the aircraft. SP recognized the ambiguity within about five seconds, stated positive retention of control, assigned the Check List reading to IP and then declared the emergency and the intentions in full, without prompting.
texts.3: SP coordinated the handling of the emergency with IP throughout. Control of the aircraft and the reading of the procedure were assigned explicitly, the emergency was declared to ATC in plain language and the intentions were passed clearly and in time.
texts.4: SP assigned roles in the first seconds after the indication, retained control explicitly and kept IP informed of the aircraft state, the procedure step in progress and the intended recovery. The emergency declaration and the request to ATC were made in plain language, complete at the first transmission and correctly timed against the workload of the procedure.
texts.marginal: SP assigned roles and declared the emergency within standards, but the intentions were passed only after the procedure had been completed rather than as the plan developed. The tendency is toward working the problem in isolation and briefing the other cockpit afterwards. SP is expected to keep a running plain-language exchange on aircraft state and intentions during the procedure, not after it.

texts_at.1: SP coordinated the execution of the procedure with IP inside the code 1 band, control and task allocation made clear only after each element was prompted. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to keep a running plain-language exchange on aircraft state and intentions during the procedure, not after it.
texts_at.2: SP coordinated the execution of the procedure with IP inside the code 2 band, correcting an ambiguity over who was flying recognized within seconds. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to state positive control at the very first indication rather than a few seconds into it.
texts_at.3: SP coordinated the handling of the emergency with IP throughout, with control of the aircraft and the reading of the procedure assigned explicitly and the emergency declared to ATC in plain language, with intentions passed a little later on one occasion than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to pass that update as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized an ambiguity over control within seconds, stated positive retention of control, assigned the Check List reading to IP and then declared the emergency and intentions in full without prompting. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to good crew coordination and declaration of the emergency.
texts_above.3: SP coordinated the handling of the emergency with IP throughout, with control of the aircraft and the reading of the procedure assigned explicitly, the emergency declared to ATC in plain language and the intentions passed clearly and in time. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to very good crew coordination and declaration of the emergency.
texts_above.4: SP assigned roles in the first seconds after the indication, retained control explicitly and kept IP informed of the aircraft state, the procedure step in progress and the intended recovery throughout. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to excellent crew coordination and declaration of the emergency.

error_modes.label: RECOGNITION AND CORRECT SELECTION OF THE PROCEDURE

texts.0: SP, due to a startle response that displaced the memorized recovery sequence, did not identify the malfunction correctly and applied the wrong critical action procedure to the indication presented. The steps actioned did not address the failure and the correct procedure was never started, leaving the aircraft in the same condition some forty seconds after the indication appeared. IP had to identify the malfunction, stop the incorrect actions and direct the applicable procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to surprise at the unannounced malfunction, did not diagnose the indication within the time the procedure requires. SP announced the wrong system first and reached the correct procedure about twenty seconds after the indication appeared, and only after IP directed attention to the actual annunciation. The correct steps were then executed, but the delay placed the response at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief startle response at the onset of the abnormal indication, hesitated for about five seconds before naming the malfunction. SP then confirmed the indication against the relevant instruments, identified the correct procedure without prompting and began the memory items with no further delay. Diagnosis and selection of the procedure were correct at the first statement.
texts.3: SP recognized the abnormal indication immediately, identified the malfunction correctly and selected the applicable procedure without hesitation. Confirmation against the associated instruments was made before the first memory item was actioned, and the response was both accurate and timely.
texts.4: SP identified every malfunction presented within a second of the indication appearing, confirmed it against the associated instruments and named the applicable procedure before beginning the memory items. SP remained composed on the unannounced failures and distinguished correctly between two similar indications that call for different procedures.
texts.marginal: SP identified the malfunctions correctly and inside the required time, but the response to the first unannounced indication began with a visible pause before the diagnosis was stated. The tendency is toward a startle reaction that consumes the first seconds of a procedure in which those seconds matter. SP is expected to practise the recognition and confirmation sequence so the response becomes immediate regardless of when the malfunction is introduced.

texts_at.1: SP identified the malfunction and selected the applicable procedure inside the code 1 band, the correct procedure reached only after attention was directed to the actual annunciation. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to practise the recognition and confirmation sequence so the response becomes immediate regardless of when the malfunction is introduced.
texts_at.2: SP identified the malfunction and selected the applicable procedure inside the code 2 band, correcting a brief hesitation before naming the malfunction on the first unannounced indication. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to shorten that hesitation so the name is given at once.
texts_at.3: SP recognized the abnormal indication immediately, identified the malfunction correctly and selected the applicable procedure without hesitation, confirming against the associated instruments before the first memory item on all but one occasion. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to confirm that one occasion just as promptly.

texts_above.2: SP confirmed the indication against the relevant instruments after a brief hesitation, identified the correct procedure without prompting and began the memory items with no further delay. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to sound recognition and selection of the procedure.
texts_above.3: SP recognized the abnormal indication immediately, identified the malfunction correctly and selected the applicable procedure without hesitation, confirming against the associated instruments before the first memory item was actioned with a response both accurate and timely. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed recognition and selection of the procedure.
texts_above.4: SP identified every malfunction presented within a second of the indication appearing, confirmed it against the associated instruments and named the applicable procedure before beginning the memory items, remaining composed on the unannounced failures. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exceptional recognition and selection of the procedure.

error_modes.label: CWS PANEL SCAN BEFORE RESETTING THE MASTER WARNING / CAUTION LIGHT

texts.0: SP, due to a reflex push of the MASTER WARNING / CAUTION light before the CWS panel had been looked at, extinguished the indication without reading which capsule was illuminated. The failed system was then named from the tone alone, no confirmation was requested from the other crewmember and the wrong system was worked for about forty seconds. IP had to reconstruct which capsule had illuminated and identify the malfunction before the correct procedure could be started.
texts.1: SP, due to resetting the light after only a partial look at the CWS panel, read one illuminated capsule and missed the second one that was already on. The malfunction was identified about fifteen seconds after the indication and only after IP asked which capsules had been seen. All indications were then considered and the correct procedure was run, but the diagnosis was completed at the limit of the acceptable delay and with verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to reaching for the reset before completing the scan, started to silence the indication with the CWS panel still unread. SP stopped the movement before pressing, read both illuminated capsules, confirmed them with the other crewmember and only then reset the light. The interruption cost about five seconds and no input from IP was required.
texts.3: SP looked at the CWS panel before pushing the MASTER WARNING / CAUTION light on every indication presented. The illuminated capsules were read aloud and confirmed with the other crewmember, and all indications were considered in the diagnosis before any capsule was extinguished.
texts.4: SP read the complete CWS panel on each activation, called the illuminated capsules and the order in which they came on, obtained confirmation from the other crewmember and reset the light only afterwards. SP also cross-checked the associated engine and system instruments before naming the malfunction, and detected a second capsule that illuminated later in the sequence without losing track of the first.
texts.marginal: SP scanned the CWS panel before every reset and named the capsules correctly, but on two occasions the scan stopped at the first illuminated capsule and was extended only on a second look. The tendency is to reset in order to silence the indication rather than to complete the diagnosis first, which will cost information whenever more than one system is affected. SP is expected to read the whole panel and confirm it with the other crewmember before the reset is pressed.

texts_at.1: SP looked at the CWS panel before resetting the MASTER WARNING / CAUTION light inside the code 1 band, all indications considered only after IP asked which capsules had been seen. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to read the whole panel and confirm it with the other crewmember before the reset is pressed.
texts_at.2: SP looked at the CWS panel before resetting the MASTER WARNING / CAUTION light inside the code 2 band, correcting a reach for the reset stopped before the panel had been fully read. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to complete the scan before the hand moves toward the reset.
texts_at.3: SP looked at the CWS panel before pushing the MASTER WARNING / CAUTION light on every indication presented, reading the illuminated capsules aloud and confirming them with the other crewmember, with one scan extended on a second look before it was confirmed. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to complete that scan on the first look as well.

texts_above.2: SP stopped the movement toward the reset before pressing, read both illuminated capsules, confirmed them with the other crewmember and only then reset the light, with no input from IP required. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady CWS panel scan discipline.
texts_above.3: SP looked at the CWS panel before pushing the MASTER WARNING / CAUTION light on every indication presented, reading the illuminated capsules aloud and confirming them with the other crewmember before any capsule was extinguished. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate CWS panel scan discipline.
texts_above.4: SP read the complete CWS panel on each activation, called the illuminated capsules and the order in which they came on, obtained confirmation from the other crewmember and cross-checked the associated instruments before naming the malfunction. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary CWS panel scan discipline.

error_modes.label: ANALYZE BEFORE BOLDFACE - TIME STANDS STILL AND FEVER CHECK
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 TABLETOP AND STAND-UP EMERGENCY PROCEDURES (EPS)

texts.0: SP, due to going directly to the memory items without analyzing the situation, executed a critical action procedure before the problem had been positively identified. No FEVER check was made, so fluctuating fuel flow, ITT, visual indications, erratic operation and roughness were never queried, and the PCL was moved on the basis of a single unconfirmed indication. IP had to stop the actions, run the analysis and direct the procedure that actually applied.
texts.1: SP, due to compressing the analysis to the first indication seen, began the boldface without confirming the remaining items of the FEVER check. Fuel flow was never checked against the ten pounds per hour criterion and roughness was reported only after IP asked for it, about twenty seconds into the procedure. The diagnosis eventually proved correct, but the analysis was completed at the lower limit of the standard and only with prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial move toward the memory items before the situation had been analyzed, started the procedure with the FEVER check incomplete. SP recognized this within about five seconds, held the actions, queried fluctuating fuel flow, ITT, visual indications, erratic operation and roughness in turn, and then executed the correct boldface with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP used the analysis step before any memory item was actioned, treating the flight condition as stable enough to allow it. The FEVER check was run in full, the indications were confirmed with the other crewmember and the boldface was started only after the malfunction had been positively identified.
texts.4: SP stabilized the aircraft, then analyzed the situation with a complete FEVER check, comparing fuel flow against the ten pounds per hour criterion and checking ITT, visual indications, erratic operation and roughness before naming the malfunction. The applicable boldface was stated and only then executed, and SP kept the analysis to the time actually needed rather than extending it.
texts.marginal: SP analyzed the situation before every boldface and reached the correct diagnosis, but the analysis was extended well past the point at which the malfunction was already evident. The tendency is to keep collecting indications in order to gain thinking time, and time does not stand still in the aircraft as it does in the flight room. SP is expected to close the analysis and act once the failure has been identified.

texts_at.1: SP analyzed the situation with a FEVER check before any memory item was actioned inside the code 1 band, roughness reported only after it was asked for. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to close the analysis and act once the failure has been identified.
texts_at.2: SP analyzed the situation with a FEVER check before any memory item was actioned inside the code 2 band, correcting an incomplete check recognized within seconds before the boldface. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to complete the check before the first move toward the memory items.
texts_at.3: SP used the analysis step before any memory item was actioned, treating the flight condition as stable enough to allow it, running the FEVER check in full and confirming the indications with the other crewmember before starting the boldface, with one analysis extended slightly past the point of certainty. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to close that analysis as promptly as the rest.

texts_above.2: SP recognized an incomplete FEVER check within seconds, held the actions, queried the remaining items in turn and then executed the correct boldface with no input from IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable analysis before boldface.
texts_above.3: SP used the analysis step before any memory item was actioned, treating the flight condition as stable enough to allow it, running the FEVER check in full and confirming the indications with the other crewmember before the boldface was started. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good analysis before boldface.

The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior analysis before boldface.

error_modes.label: POST-BOLDFACE VERIFICATION LOOP AND RETURN TO A/C CONTROL
error_modes.source: technique:1.21 TABLETOP AND STAND-UP EMERGENCY PROCEDURES (EPS)

texts.0: SP, due to treating the memory items as the end of the procedure, did not verify whether the boldface had done what it was intended to do and never asked whether a further boldface applied. No second FEVER check was made and the PCL was brought below 60 % without any compensation on stick, rudder and PCL, so the aircraft ended about 600 feet low with 20 degrees of heading change. IP had to recover the aircraft state and direct the follow-on procedure that had been missed.
texts.1: SP, due to moving straight from the boldface into the cleanup items, did not re-analyze the effect of the actions taken. The second FEVER check was made about twenty seconds late and only after IP asked whether the malfunction had responded, and by then the aircraft had drifted some 250 feet low with airspeed 15 knots below the briefed value. The loop was then closed correctly, but at the limit of the acceptable standard and with verbal prompting.
texts.2: SP, due to a short omission at the end of the memory items, initially went on without checking the result of the boldface. SP caught this within about five seconds, re-checked the engine indications, confirmed that the action had produced the intended effect, asked whether another boldface applied and re-trimmed the aircraft after the power change, with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP closed the loop after every critical action procedure: the aircraft state was checked first, the indications were re-analyzed to confirm the boldface had worked, and the question of whether another boldface applied was raised before moving on. Power and trim were reset after each configuration change so control was maintained throughout.
texts.4: SP returned to aircraft control after every boldface and every checklist, re-ran the FEVER check to confirm the action had produced the intended effect and explicitly stated when no further boldface applied. When the PCL was reduced, SP compensated on stick, rudder and PCL and re-trimmed before continuing, with no measurable change in altitude, airspeed or heading.
texts.marginal: SP verified the effect of each boldface and re-checked aircraft control, but the verification was made after the whole sequence rather than after each individual action. The tendency is to run the memory items as one block and audit the result at the end, which will hide a step that did not achieve its purpose. SP is expected to close the analyze - act - verify loop after each single action in the coming sorties.

texts_at.1: SP verified the effect of the boldface and checked whether a further one applied inside the code 1 band, the second FEVER check made only after it was asked whether the malfunction had responded. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to close the analyze - act - verify loop after each single action in the coming sorties.
texts_at.2: SP verified the effect of the boldface and checked whether a further one applied inside the code 2 band, correcting an omission caught within seconds before moving on. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to check the result of each action before it is assumed complete.
texts_at.3: SP closed the loop after every critical action procedure, checking aircraft state first, re-analyzing the indications to confirm the boldface had worked and asking whether another boldface applied, with one verification run a little later than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to run that verification as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP caught an omission within seconds, re-checked the engine indications, confirmed the action had produced the intended effect, asked whether another boldface applied and re-trimmed the aircraft with no input from IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured post-boldface verification.
texts_above.3: SP closed the loop after every critical action procedure: aircraft state checked first, indications re-analyzed to confirm the boldface had worked, and the question of whether another boldface applied raised before moving on, with power and trim reset after each configuration change. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise post-boldface verification.
texts_above.4: SP returned to aircraft control after every boldface and every checklist, re-ran the FEVER check to confirm the action had produced the intended effect and explicitly stated when no further boldface applied. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate post-boldface verification.

error_modes.label: PEL INITIAL ACTIONS - TURN, CLIMB, CLEAN, CHECK, BIP

texts.0: SP, due to delaying the turn to the nearest suitable field while the indication was still being discussed, held the original heading for more than a minute after the malfunction appeared. Gear, flaps and speed brake were left extended, so the glide ratio stayed near 1.5:1 instead of 2:1 and the aircraft ended well below the altitude required for High Key. IP had to take control, turn toward the field and clean up the aircraft.
texts.1: SP, due to a late start of the initial actions, turned toward the nearest suitable field about thirty seconds after the malfunction and left the speed brake extended through the first part of the climb. The cleanup and the BIP step were completed only after IP called them, and the profile was intercepted about 200 feet below High Key, at the lower limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a short hesitation over field selection, held the heading for about ten seconds before turning. SP then applied the sequence in order, raised gear, flaps and speed brake, cross-checked the indications and set the boost pump and ignition switches as required, intercepting the profile at High Key with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP turned immediately toward the nearest suitable field, climbed as the energy state allowed, cleaned up the aircraft, cross-checked all indications and set the boost pump and ignition switches as required. The profile was intercepted at High Key with the aircraft clean and on the glide speed.
texts.4: SP turned toward the selected field within a few seconds of the malfunction, stating the reason for the choice, and completed the cleanup before the climb had ended so no excess drag remained. All indications were cross-checked while the profile was being intercepted, the BIP step was set as required, and SP arrived at High Key with altitude in hand and a stated plan for the pattern.
texts.marginal: SP applied all the initial actions in the correct order and reached the profile within standards, but the memory aid was recited some way ahead of the actions themselves and the cleanup lagged the turn by several seconds each time. The tendency is to run the sequence as a spoken list rather than as immediate actions, and in a real power loss the delay comes straight out of the glide range. SP is expected to fly the sequence as it is called in the coming sorties.

texts_at.1: SP turned toward the nearest suitable field and ran the turn, climb, clean, check, BIP sequence inside the code 1 band, the cleanup and BIP step completed only after they were called. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to fly the sequence as it is called in the coming sorties.
texts_at.2: SP turned toward the nearest suitable field and ran the turn, climb, clean, check, BIP sequence inside the code 2 band, correcting a short hesitation over field selection before the sequence was applied in order. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to shorten that hesitation so the turn begins even sooner.
texts_at.3: SP turned immediately toward the nearest suitable field, climbed as the energy state allowed, cleaned up the aircraft, cross-checked all indications and set the boost pump and ignition switches as required, with the memory aid recited a little ahead of the actions on one occasion. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to keep the actions and the aid together on that occasion as well.

texts_above.2: SP applied the sequence in order after a short hesitation over field selection, raising gear, flaps and speed brake, cross-checking indications and setting the boost pump and ignition switches with no input from IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to solid PEL initial-actions sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP turned immediately toward the nearest suitable field, climbed as the energy state allowed, cleaned up the aircraft, cross-checked all indications and set the boost pump and ignition switches as required, intercepting the profile at High Key with the aircraft clean and on the glide speed. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to well-developed PEL initial-actions sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP turned toward the selected field within a few seconds of the malfunction, stating the reason for the choice, and completed the cleanup before the climb had ended so no excess drag remained. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to outstanding PEL initial-actions sequencing.

error_modes.label: ZOOM CLIMB ENERGY TRADE AND GLIDE PROFILE TRIM

texts.0: SP, due to omitting the trade of excess airspeed for altitude, kept the aircraft at more than 150 KIAS after the power loss and made no zoom climb. About 500 feet of available altitude were given away and the airspeed was then allowed to decay below the 125 knot glide speed with the power never set to the 4 - 6 % torque of the profile. IP had to take control to restore the glide speed and the profile.
texts.1: SP, due to a shallow and late zoom, pulled to about 10 degrees of climb instead of 20 and lowered the nose some 35 KIAS above the desired glide airspeed. The aircraft ended about 200 feet below the profile and the trim was set for the glide only after IP called the airspeed twice, leaving the manoeuvre at the limit of the acceptable standard.
texts.2: SP, due to an initial pull of about 1.5 G, converted less of the excess airspeed than the technique allows and reached roughly 15 degrees of climb angle. SP recognized the shallow profile before the airspeed had decayed, corrected the attitude, lowered the nose approaching 20 KIAS above the glide speed and trimmed for 125 knots with 4 - 6 % torque, ending within about 100 feet of the profile and with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP initiated the zoom climb above 150 KIAS with a 2-G pull to a 20 degree climb angle, lowered the nose approaching 20 KIAS above the desired glide airspeed and trimmed for a 125 knot minimum descent with 4 - 6 % torque. The profile was intercepted on speed and on altitude.
texts.4: SP traded the excess airspeed exactly as briefed, holding 2 G to a 20 degree climb angle and starting the recovery within a few knots of 20 KIAS above the glide speed. Power was reduced to 4 - 6 % torque and the aircraft was trimmed hands-off at the glide airspeed, with the resulting altitude matching the ten knots for one hundred feet trade within a negligible margin.
texts.marginal: SP flew the zoom climb and reached the glide profile inside the required parameters, but the aircraft was held on the glide speed by continuous stick pressure rather than trimmed for it. The tendency is to leave the trim unfinished after the energy trade, and the airspeed starts to drift as soon as attention moves to the checklist. SP is expected to complete the trim for the glide speed before turning to the next step.

texts_at.1: SP traded the excess airspeed for altitude in the zoom climb inside the code 1 band, the trim for the glide airspeed set only after IP called the airspeed twice. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to complete the trim for the glide speed before turning to the next step.
texts_at.2: SP traded the excess airspeed for altitude in the zoom climb inside the code 2 band, correcting a shallow initial climb angle recognized before the airspeed had decayed. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to hold closer to the full 2 G pull so the climb angle needs no correction.
texts_at.3: SP initiated the zoom climb above 150 KIAS with a 2-G pull to a 20 degree climb angle, lowered the nose approaching 20 KIAS above the desired glide airspeed and trimmed for the glide with 4 to 6 percent torque, with the trim finished a little later on one climb than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to finish that trim as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a shallow profile before the airspeed had decayed, corrected the attitude, lowered the nose toward the target and trimmed for the glide speed with no input from IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady zoom-climb energy trade technique.
texts_above.3: SP initiated the zoom climb above 150 KIAS with a 2-G pull to a 20 degree climb angle, lowered the nose approaching 20 KIAS above the desired glide airspeed and trimmed for a 125 knot minimum descent with 4 to 6 percent torque, intercepting the profile on speed and on altitude. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate zoom-climb energy trade technique.
texts_above.4: SP traded the excess airspeed exactly as briefed, holding 2 G to a 20 degree climb angle and starting the recovery within a few knots of the target, trimming the aircraft hands-off at the glide airspeed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary zoom-climb energy trade technique.

error_modes.label: ORM 3-2-1 DESCENT GATES AND CONTINUE OR EJECT DECISION

texts.0: SP, due to pressing on with a recovery that was no longer supported by the energy state, descended below 2000 feet AGL while off profile and without the runway in sight. No minimum ejection altitude had been set, the continue or eject decision was never made at 300 feet AGL and the aircraft was still displaced from the centerline passing 100 feet AGL. IP had to take control and terminate the pattern.
texts.1: SP, due to accepting a profile that was marginally low, passed 2000 feet AGL only just on profile and with the runway acquired late. The continue decision at 300 feet AGL was stated after the altitude had been passed and the gear was confirmed and reported at about 150 feet AGL, both after IP called for them, leaving the gates met only at the limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to a slightly steep intercept, approached 2000 feet AGL marginally off profile with the runway in sight. SP recognized the deviation before the gate, adjusted the pattern back onto profile and then made the continue decision at 300 feet AGL, confirmed and reported the gear at 200 feet AGL and was aligned with the centerline by 100 feet AGL, with no input from IP.
texts.3: SP applied the ORM 3-2-1 gates as briefed, descending below 2000 feet AGL only when on profile, with the runway in sight and in a position to manoeuvre safely to land. The continue or eject decision was made at 300 feet AGL, the gear was confirmed and reported at 200 feet AGL and the aircraft was aligned with the centerline at 100 feet AGL.
texts.4: SP stated the criteria for each gate as it was reached and met all three with margin, arriving on profile with the runway in sight well before 2000 feet AGL. The continue decision at 300 feet AGL was made against explicit criteria rather than as a call, the gear was confirmed and reported at 200 feet AGL and the alignment at 100 feet AGL required no correction on final.
texts.marginal: SP met every ORM 3-2-1 gate and reported them on altitude, but the 300 foot decision was voiced as a routine call with no reference to the energy state or the position relative to the runway. The tendency is to treat the gates as reporting points rather than as decision points, and that is what removes the ejection option when the profile actually deteriorates. SP is expected to state the criteria being assessed at each gate in the coming sorties.

texts_at.1: SP applied the ORM 3-2-1 gates as briefed inside the code 1 band, the continue decision and the gear confirmation both made only after IP called for them. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to state the criteria being assessed at each gate in the coming sorties.
texts_at.2: SP applied the ORM 3-2-1 gates as briefed inside the code 2 band, correcting a slightly steep intercept recognized before the 2000 foot gate. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to recognize that intercept a little earlier so the adjustment is smaller.
texts_at.3: SP applied the ORM 3-2-1 gates as briefed, descending below 2000 feet AGL only when on profile with the runway in sight, making the continue decision at 300 feet AGL and confirming the gear at 200 feet AGL, with the centerline alignment reached a little later on one approach than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to reach that alignment as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP recognized a deviation before the 2000 foot gate, adjusted the pattern back onto profile and then made the continue decision, the gear confirmation and the centerline alignment with no input from IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to dependable use of the ORM 3-2-1 descent gates.
texts_above.3: SP applied the ORM 3-2-1 gates as briefed, descending below 2000 feet AGL only when on profile with the runway in sight and in a position to manoeuvre safely to land, making the continue decision at 300 feet AGL and confirming the gear and the centerline alignment at their gates. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to notably good use of the ORM 3-2-1 descent gates.
texts_above.4: SP stated the criteria for each gate as it was reached and met all three with margin, arriving on profile with the runway in sight well before 2000 feet AGL and needing no correction on final. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to superior use of the ORM 3-2-1 descent gates.

error_modes.label: TAKEOFF ABORT DECISION AND PNF WARNING CALL

texts.0: SP, due to hesitating when there was a clear reason to abort, kept the PCL advanced for more than five seconds after the malfunction appeared on the takeoff roll. No abort was called, the hazardous indication seen from the rear cockpit was never passed to the other pilot and the aircraft continued to accelerate toward the rotation speed. IP had to take control, call the abort and carry out the procedure.
texts.1: SP, due to weighing whether the takeoff could still be continued, called the abort about three seconds after the reason to abort was evident. The indication was passed to the other cockpit only after IP asked what had been seen, and the decision was made at the limit of the acceptable delay for the runway remaining.
texts.2: SP, due to a brief hesitation at the onset of the indication, delayed the decision by about one second before calling the abort. SP then stated the abort clearly, informed the other cockpit of what had been seen and executed the procedure without any prompting from IP, with the aircraft stopped well inside the runway remaining.
texts.3: SP did not hesitate when there was reason to abort: the decision was made immediately, the abort was called clearly and the hazardous indication was passed to the other pilot as it was seen. The procedure was then executed according to the Check List.
texts.4: SP called and executed the abort as soon as the reason to abort appeared, passing the indication to the other cockpit in the same transmission. SP also stated the stopping plan and the follow-on intentions - clearing the runway or stopping in place for a ground inspection - without being asked, and remained ready to hand over or take control as the situation required.
texts.marginal: SP aborted inside the time and distance available and passed the indication to the other cockpit, but the decision was visibly weighed against completing the takeoff before it was made. The tendency is to look for a reason to continue when the criteria to abort have already been met, and on a shorter runway that pause would be decisive. SP is expected to make the abort call the moment the criteria are met, without further consideration.

texts_at.1: SP called the takeoff abort and passed the reason to the other cockpit inside the code 1 band, the decision made at the limit of the acceptable delay for the runway remaining. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to make the abort call the moment the criteria are met, without further consideration.
texts_at.2: SP called the takeoff abort and passed the reason to the other cockpit inside the code 2 band, correcting a brief hesitation before calling the abort. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to shorten that hesitation so the call and the indication are passed together.
texts_at.3: SP did not hesitate when there was reason to abort, calling the abort clearly and passing the hazardous indication to the other pilot as it was seen before executing the procedure according to the Check List, with one call made a moment later than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to make that call as promptly as the others.

texts_above.2: SP stated the abort clearly after a brief hesitation, informed the other cockpit of what had been seen and executed the procedure without any prompting from IP, stopping well inside the runway remaining. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to assured takeoff abort decision-making.
texts_above.3: SP showed no hesitation when there was reason to abort: the decision was made immediately, the abort was called clearly and the hazardous indication was passed to the other pilot as it was seen, with the procedure then executed according to the Check List. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to precise takeoff abort decision-making.
texts_above.4: SP called and executed the abort as soon as the reason to abort appeared, passing the indication to the other cockpit in the same transmission and stating the stopping plan and the follow-on intentions without being asked. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to first-rate takeoff abort decision-making.

error_modes.label: EMERGENCY GROUND EGRESS SEQUENCE AND GROUND CREW COORDINATION
error_modes.source: technique:3.15 ABNORMAL PROCEDURES (INCL. 3.15.1 EMERGENCY GROUND EGRESS, 3.15.2 RETURN TO APRON)

texts.0: SP, due to reacting to the ground emergency without following the systematic and deliberate sequence, began the egress before the aircraft had been brought to a complete stop and with the parking brake unset. The battery and generator were turned OFF at the start, so the intercom with the other cockpit was lost, the ISS was left out of SOLO and no seat pin was installed. IP had to stop the sequence and complete the egress items in order.
texts.1: SP, due to running the egress items out of the printed order, moved the battery and generator to OFF before the seat pins had been installed and lost the intercom with the other cockpit at the last step. The controlling agency was informed about thirty seconds late and only after IP directed the call, leaving the sequence complete but at the limit of the standard.
texts.2: SP, due to the pace of the first actions, reached for the battery switch before the ISS had been placed in SOLO. SP stopped, set the parking brake, shut down the engine, placed the ISS in SOLO, installed both seat pins and only then turned the battery and generator OFF, keeping the intercom available up to the egress and requiring no input from IP.
texts.3: SP performed the emergency ground egress in a systematic and deliberate manner: complete stop, parking brake set, engine shut down, ISS in SOLO, both seat pins installed and battery and generator OFF just before egress. The controlling agency was informed and no switch was actuated without the ground crew being told.
texts.4: SP ran the egress in order and at a controlled pace, keeping the intercom with the other cockpit alive until the last action and announcing each step as it was completed. SP notified the controlling agency that assistance was required, set the parking brake and raised both hands to signal hands clear for the inspection, and confirmed that both seat pins were installed before leaving the cockpit.
texts.marginal: SP completed every egress item in the printed order and coordinated with the other cockpit, but the pace was hurried and two switches were selected before the corresponding call had been answered. The tendency is toward speed at the expense of the deliberate sequence, which is where the seat pins and the ISS position get missed. SP is expected to hold the announced pace and confirm each item with the other cockpit before moving on.

texts_at.1: SP performed the emergency ground egress in the printed order inside the code 1 band, the controlling agency informed about thirty seconds late and only after IP directed the call. Performance met the desired standard for this stage, and SP is expected to hold the announced pace and confirm each item with the other cockpit before moving on.
texts_at.2: SP performed the emergency ground egress in the printed order inside the code 2 band, correcting a reach for the battery switch stopped before the ISS had been placed in SOLO. Performance remained inside the standard required for this stage of training, and SP is expected to pace the first actions a little more deliberately so the pause is not needed.
texts_at.3: SP performed the emergency ground egress in a systematic and deliberate manner, coordinating each action with the other cockpit, with a complete stop, parking brake set, engine shut down and both seat pins installed before the battery and generator were turned off, with the controlling agency informed a little later on one drill than the rest. The result is in line with the proficiency expected at this point of the syllabus, and SP is expected to inform them as promptly as on the others.

texts_above.2: SP stopped before reaching for the battery switch, set the parking brake, shut down the engine, placed the ISS in SOLO and installed both seat pins before turning the battery and generator off, requiring no input from IP. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to steady emergency ground egress sequencing.
texts_above.3: SP performed the emergency ground egress in a systematic and deliberate manner: complete stop, parking brake set, engine shut down, ISS in SOLO, both seat pins installed and battery and generator OFF just before egress, with the controlling agency informed and no switch actuated without the ground crew being told. Performance was above the level required at this point of the syllabus, due to consistently accurate emergency ground egress sequencing.
texts_above.4: SP ran the egress in order and at a controlled pace, keeping the intercom with the other cockpit alive until the last action and announcing each step as it was completed. The result is above the code required for this Training Section, due to exemplary emergency ground egress sequencing.
